questions.explanation: What the crew needed was the critical incident stress debriefing: a formal, structured group session, usually held 24 to 72 hours after the incident and led by a trained peer-and-mental-health team, where responders talk through the incident and their reactions under ground rules of confidentiality. It is deliberately kept separate from any critique of tactics or performance — the captain's meeting was an operational review wearing the wrong name. A defusing is the short, informal session held within hours of the call, an employee assistance program is an ongoing counseling resource rather than a single session, and critical incident stress management is the name of the whole program the debriefing sits inside.
questions.question: After a fatal apartment fire, a captain holds a meeting the next evening and calls it the crew's debriefing. Hold the identical formal session again every week until the symptoms stop.

Nothing further; once the formal session has been held, the agency's responsibility is finished.

questions.question: Your crew went through the formal group session two days after a child's death, but a month later two members are still having nightmares, trouble concentrating, and dread about coming to work. What should the agency do next?

questions.question: After a 1989 earthquake in Newcastle, Australia, researchers followed 195 disaster helpers for 2 years, comparing 62 who were debriefed with 133 who were not. choices: bacterial pneumonia
bronchitis
tuberculosis

questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is caused by a slow-growing airborne bacterium — identified by Robert Koch in 1882 — whose waxy coat lets it survive inside tiny dried droplet nuclei floating in shared air. Because it grows slowly, the illness builds over weeks rather than days, which rules out influenza and ordinary pneumonia, both of which peak fast. The immune system's long fight against it produces the drenching night sweats and the weight loss, and as the infection hollows out a cavity in the lung it can erode a small blood vessel, which is where the blood-streaked sputum comes from. Bronchitis inflames the airways but does not cavitate lung tissue or waste the body this way. The same airborne biology is why the crew wears a fit-tested respirator and the patient wears a mask.

Droplet precautions only: a surgical mask on the crew is enough for any coughing patient.
questions.explanation: An airborne disease that spreads through shared room air calls for airborne precautions — respirator for the crew, mask on the patient, fresh air in the unit. Droplet and contact precautions aim at splashes and touch, which are not how this infection travels.
